evidence: HB 3546 (POWER Act, 2025) created a large-energy-use rate class (20 MW+); OPUC approved PGE Schedule 96 in Order 26-239 (docket UM 2377, 2026-07-10) and approved a Pacific Power large-load tariff in 2024 (UE 433).
pending: Pacific Power updated data-center tariff (UE 463) decision expected late 2026.

evidence: POWER Act sets a 10-year minimum contract (scaling up with load, reported up to 30 years); PGE rules reportedly require paying for 90% of contracted demand regardless of use, with exceedance penalties and exit fees for abandoned or closed facilities.
Rules require long-term contracts, exit fees and stranded-asset protection for PGE data-center customers; specific collateral or deposit amounts were not found in sources reviewed.
pending: Details being set in UM 2377 and UE 463.

evidence: POWER Act makes data centers/crypto (20 MW+) bear their cost of service via a separate class; PGE order requires them to pay for clean energy their load needs, a 1 cent/kWh surcharge at 100 MW+, and interconnection only once clean energy is available.

Gov. Kotek on 2026-09-08 paused state-land sales, easements, leases and land-use permits for data centers (reported through 2027-07-01) and said she supports a statewide moratorium, which needs the Legislature; Hillsboro adopted a 120-day local pause on 2026-07-27 and four Democratic legislators plan a 3-year moratorium bill for 2027.
pending: 2027 Legislature may act on a statewide moratorium; DCAC final report due Oct 2026.

evidence: Siting runs through local land-use approval under Oregon's statewide planning system with public hearings; no state siting certificate exists for data centers (EFSC covers energy facilities only).
State POWER Act obligations are triggered at 20 MW (large energy use facilities, NAICS 518210), well under 100 MW.
DEQ runs a Tier 4 fast-track air permit pathway for data centers (standard permit template, no site-specific dispersion modeling) that shortens processing.
Oregon has no general sales tax.

HB 4084 (eff. 2026-06-05) bars new data centers from the Enterprise Zones property tax program until 90 days after the 2027 session; existing and already-approved projects are grandfathered and the Strategic Investment Program remains available.
pending: Could lapse or be extended after the 2027 session.

evidence: Enterprise Zone/SIP abatements carry local job, wage and community-fee conditions (Hillsboro reviewing its community impact fee); not a statewide clawback regime.
No data-center-specific water reporting or withdrawal limit found; advocates note mitigation is inconsistent or absent and are asking OPUC and the advisory committee for water reporting.
pending: Data Center Advisory Committee water dialogue may yield recommendations.

evidence: DEQ's data-center permit path uses Cleaner Air Oregon risk screening with annual/daily fuel limits and a 50 lb/hr NOx testing threshold; Tier 4-level controls are required only on the fast-track route.
Oregon has no SEPA/CEQA-type general environmental review statute applying to data centers.
No mandatory curtailment, demand-response or on-site generation limit specific to data centers found.
Labor/job and wage conditions arise through Enterprise Zone/SIP incentive agreements rather than statute for data centers.
POWER Act requires data-center operators to report energy usage in annual reports; no statutory water or emissions reporting.
No statewide noise or setback standard specific to data centers found.
Pacific Power rules (UE 463) pending, Kotek backing a statewide moratorium, a 3-year moratorium bill planned for 2027 and advisory committee recommendations due late 2026.
PGE said 16 existing data centers are immediately affected by the new class and Portland market growth is straining supply; no formal queue backlog figure found.

UTC opened docket UE-260162 (Apr 2026) toward a large-load interconnection policy statement for investor-owned utilities; no statewide IOU data-center class yet, though consumer-owned PUDs (Chelan, Grant, Douglas) have separate large-load/crypto rates and a 50-state survey lists Washington as having approved tariffs.
pending: UTC policy statement expected after a 6-8 month process; workgroup Rec. 2 calls for a model large-load class.

evidence: No statewide minimum-bill or term requirement; workgroup lists contract-term and minimum off-take as options only.
No large-load collateral rule adopted; workgroup finding lists credit commitments and service-extension charges as options.

HB 2515 (large-load tariffs, curtailment, reporting) passed the House but died in the Senate in 2026; SB 5982 passed, making large customers including data centers meet the same clean-energy deadlines as utilities.
pending: HB 2515 sponsor plans to reintroduce in 2027.

evidence: As of Sept 2026 about 30 local moratoria are in force in Washington, including Seattle, Spokane (city and county), Snohomish, Pierce (10 MW+), Skagit and Yakima counties; no statewide pause.
No state siting board; projects go through local land-use approval and SEPA with public process.
No state review threshold in force; the 20 MW definition in HB 2515 did not pass.
Ecology has a draft area-specific general order to streamline emergency-engine air permits in the Quincy/Wenatchee area, but it is not confirmed final; no special fast-track program.

Rural and non-rural data-center sales/use tax exemptions remain but SB 6231 (eff. July 2026) limits them to original equipment and ends refurbishment exemptions; six counties are excluded from the non-rural program.
Washington has no property tax incentive for data centers.
The workgroup report does not describe job, wage or clawback conditions on the exemptions; a recommendation tying tax preferences to clean energy was not adopted.
No enacted data-center water reporting or limits; workgroup Rec. 4 (annual water reporting) was adopted as a recommendation and HB 2515's disclosures failed.
Ecology's draft area-specific general order would cap hours and fuel use and require Tier 4-equivalent emission limits for up to 21 engines per site.
SEPA applies to data center projects (Ecology issued a SEPA determination of non-significance for the generator general order).
No mandatory data-center curtailment or on-site generation limit enacted; HB 2515's emergency curtailment tariffs died.
No labor conditions are attached to the data-center exemptions found.
SB 5982 directs the UTC to set reporting so large customers can demonstrate clean-energy compliance; broader energy/water disclosure failed.
No statewide data-center noise or setback rule found.
Comprehensive data-center legislation was deferred to 2027, the workgroup final report is delayed, UTC docket UE-260162 is open, and local moratoria are spreading.
PSE reports large-load requests above 20 MW in 2025 equal almost 50% of its peak load, and a new large-load process is still being developed.

Package signed 2026-09-21 (AB 2383, SB 886, SB 1168) requires the CPUC to create a separate data-center/large-load rate class and tariffs, effective generally 2027; PG&E's Rule 30 transmission-level large-load tariff is also before the CPUC.
pending: Tariffs still to be written by CPUC; Rule 30 decision pending.

evidence: SB 886 as drafted called for 15-year contracts and early-termination fees; enacted terms were not confirmed in sources reviewed.
PG&E's Rule 30 proposal has large-load customers fund projects upfront with repayment after load arrives; SB 886 drafts required prefunding; deposit amounts unknown.

Enacted AB 2383 and SB 886 direct the CPUC to make qualifying data centers bear transmission, distribution, generation and energization costs; SB 57 (Oct 2025) first required a CPUC cost-shift study due 2027-01-01.
Dozens of local pauses exist (22 in force as of Sept 2026, including Los Angeles County, Richmond, Gilroy, Morgan Hill, Palm Springs); no statewide pause.
Local discretionary approvals plus CEQA review with public process; no state siting board for data centers.
Enacted measures use low thresholds: SB 886 reaches transmission-level data centers of 25 MW or more and AB 1577 reporting reaches 0.5 MW installed capacity (per May 2026 bill text).
CPUC streamlined transmission-level data-center interconnection for PG&E in July 2025 on an interim basis, but no formal statewide fast-track program.
California has no data-center sales tax exemption; SB 58 (partial exemption tied to renewable investment) died in committee in 2025.
No state property tax abatement for data centers found.
No state data-center incentives, so no incentive clawbacks.
AB 2469 and AB 2619 (signed 2026-09-21) require water-demand disclosure and reporting, and AB 2469 conditions local approval on developers paying for new water infrastructure; no withdrawal caps.
Backup-generator permits are handled by regional air districts with state-specific limits; no source on specific rules was retrieved.
CEQA applies; SB 887 sets a statewide data-center definition and limits categorical exemptions while offering an Environmental Leadership pathway for qualifying projects.

SB 886 drafts required demand-response participation where the CPUC authorizes it; AB 1577 requires reporting of onsite generation and demand-response participation; final mandatory terms unconfirmed.
No data-center-specific labor conditions found.
AB 1577 (signed 2026-09-21) requires qualifying data centers to report energy, PUE/WUE, onsite generation and fuel use to the CEC, with anonymized aggregated publication.
No statewide data-center noise or setback rule found.
Seven new laws take effect 2027 with CPUC, CEC and other rulemakings still to come, PG&E Rule 30 is pending and local moratoria are proliferating.
PG&E reports about 5.5 GW of data-center demand over a decade, with 1.4 GW in final design and cluster-study constraints.

SB 132 (signed 2025-03-25) defines 100 MW+ large loads for Rocky Mountain Power and the PSC is investigating a flexible large-load tariff; the first Operation Gigawatt contract was filed in Feb 2026, but no general data-center rate class has been approved.
pending: PSC large-load tariff investigation and SB 132 rulemaking (docket 25R318-01) ongoing.

evidence: Large-load service is handled through special contracts; the Operation Gigawatt agreement fully covers cost of service, but contract term and minimum-bill terms were not published in sources reviewed.
The PSC opened rulemaking 25R318-01 on SB 132 implementation (registration of self-supply customers); financial-security terms were not confirmed.

SB 132 requires grid-connected self-supply customers to pay interconnection and transmission studies, upgrades and transmission service, and the Operation Gigawatt agreement is stated to fully cover the data center's cost of service.
Nine local moratoria in force as of Sept 2026 (Box Elder, Cache, Iron, Grand, Sanpete, Wayne counties; Logan, Clearfield, Milford); no statewide pause.
Siting is by local zoning; SB 132 lets large loads pursue off-grid or separate supply without state siting approval.
SB 132's large-load provisions apply at 100 MW or more within five years.
SB 132 gives the utility 90 days to assess service; no data-center fast-track program or documented delays found.
Data centers of at least 150,000 sq ft qualify for a sales and use tax exemption (Utah Code 59-12-104).
No state property tax incentive; local incentives are used but HB 507 limits local incentives to designated zones from May 2027.
Utah attaches no wage or jobs conditions to its data-center incentive.

HB 76 (2026) requires large water users (75+ acre-feet/yr or 10,000+ sq ft) to pre-notify water needs 90-360 days before construction and file annual withdrawal reports; Salt Lake City has a local 200,000 gal/day cap.
Wasatch Front nonattainment makes generator permits state-specific, with permits limiting backup engines to emergency use; regulators say they are concerned about growth.
Utah has no state environmental review (SEPA/CEQA-type) law.
SB 132 permits closed private generation and self-supply, subject to PSC registration and NERC/WECC standards; no mandatory curtailment found.
Utah attaches no wage or jobs conditions to its data-center incentive.
HB 76 water reporting applies to large water users, but HB 585 (energy-use reporting to the PSC) failed on 2026-03-06.
The source found no statewide data-center noise or setback standards.
PSC large-load tariff investigation and SB 132 rulemaking are open, Gov. Cox issued EO 2026-03 (Data Center Framework) in May 2026, and local moratoria are spreading.
Rocky Mountain Power cannot meet rising demand; 48 data centers draw about 920 MW with about 2,600 MW under construction.

Xcel Energy filed a large-load rate class for new loads above 50 MW with the Colorado PUC in April 2026 (pending, with interveners filing May 2026); a 50-state survey lists Colorado as having approved large-load tariffs, which could not be matched to a specific order.
pending: Xcel tariff decision pending at the PUC.

evidence: Xcel's pending proposal requires 15-year minimum contracts with steep early-exit charges and a size-scaled minimum monthly bill; the PUC's resource plan decision endorsed minimum-term contracts and exit fees.
The PUC endorsed service and interconnection agreements before loads enter the forecast; collateral specifics were not found.
Cost allocation to large loads is proposed in Xcel's pending tariff and the PUC proceeding; no enacted statute or order yet.
As of Sept 2026, 25 local moratoria on data centers are in force (Denver, Boulder, Jefferson, Larimer, Broomfield and others); no statewide pause.
Siting is by local zoning (counties and municipalities); no state siting board for data centers found.
The pending Xcel tariff applies at 50 MW, and SB26-102 as introduced used 30 MW; neither is a siting review threshold.
No special fast-track program or documented statewide permitting delay found.
Colorado has no data-center sales tax exemption; HB26-1030 would create incentives but was under consideration and the Legislature postponed data-center legislation.
No state data-center property tax abatement found; local incentives not confirmed.
No state data-center incentives enacted, so no clawbacks.
No enacted data-center water reporting or limits found.
Colorado's ozone nonattainment area drives state-specific air permit limits for generators; no source on specific rules was retrieved.
Colorado has no general state environmental review statute; SB26-102's cumulative-impact analysis requirement was not enacted.
Xcel's proposal includes an optional Speed-to-Market pathway with flexible tailored contracts and an optional Clean Transition Tariff; HB26-1246 would allow bring-your-own-power.
No data-center labor conditions found.
SB26-102 would have required renewable sourcing and impact steps; the Legislature postponed data-center legislation, so no statutory reporting exists.
No statewide data-center noise or setback rule found.
Xcel tariff pending at the PUC, data-center bills (SB26-102, HB26-1030, HB26-1246) postponed, and about 25 local moratoria.
The PUC cut Xcel's requested 14 GW of new resources to about 6 GW amid large-load growth; no specific interconnection backlog figure found.
